title: On Sunk Costs (and Whether You Should Change Your Curriculum Even When You Recently Spent a Lot of Money on the Current One) hen-you-recently-spent-a-lot-of-money-on-the-current-one/
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that a district should not keep a bad curriculum simply because it recently spent money on it, since that money is a sunk cost whichever way the decision goes. The right question is whether, knowing what is known now, the district would buy that curriculum today. He urges prudence in the replacement process, with a small committee that consults research, case studies, and disinterested experts rather than polling every stakeholder, and a willingness to consider cheaper options. He lists what a bad curriculum can look like, from being superseded by better research to having incoherent vertical gaps. He closes by recommending Natalie Wexler's The Knowledge Gap as required reading before the next adoption.
points: Money already spent on a curriculum is irrecoverable and should not decide whether to keep it.
Ask whether you would adopt the curriculum today given what you now know.
Replace with prudence: a narrow, research-driven process rather than an open committee of all stakeholders.
Bad curricula include ones disproven by research, vertically clashing, or full of silo-ized gaps.
Wexler's The Knowledge Gap is offered as the foundation for any new adoption decision.
quotes: The X dollars is a sunk cost — money you can’t recover, whether you stick with the curriculum for ten more years or you abandon it tomorrow. When we continue a behavior just because we spent unrecoverable money on the behavior in the past, we engage in the sunk cost fallacy. We’re susceptible to this in all parts of life, but it’s uniquely deadly when we do it with curriculum decisions because of how many people it adversely affects.

If the answer is no, then make prudent haste in pursuing the new and better curricula. And that word prudent should be size 48 font — I mean it! This time, rethink your due diligence, e.g., don’t open-invite people to the curriculum committee.

Don’t ask for the opinions of all stakeholders — we’re in the education profession, not the please-everybody one. Consult the research, consult the case studies, consult the experts who have no money to gain from your decision but who have a reputation for helping you make a good one.
And for goodness sake, consider options that don’t cost X dollars! There are many good ones that cost a fraction of X.
